common_name: Crimson Queen Cranberry (Rutgers High-Color Processing Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring into strongly acidic, peaty, constantly moist bog soil topped with a sand layer, mimicking commercial cranberry bog conditions.

directions: Crimson Queen was bred at the Rutgers P.E. Marucci Center for Blueberry and Cranberry Research in Chatsworth, New Jersey, part of a modern breeding program aimed at combining high yield with exceptionally deep, uniform red color for the juice and processing market. Its berries carry unusually high anthocyanin content even before full ripening, which makes it attractive to processors who value color extraction over fresh-market appearance, and vines are noted for vigorous growth and heavy fruit set on established beds. Like other cranberries it demands strongly acidic soil (pH 4.0-5.0), a sandy-peat bog substrate, and constant moisture, along with periodic sand top-dressing to control weeds and encourage new rooting along runners. Home growers in cold-winter regions with the acidic, poorly drained ground cranberries require can grow it as a novelty high-pigment selection, though it is planted almost exclusively in commercial New Jersey, Wisconsin, and Quebec bogs supplying the processed cranberry market. It is unsuited to the Gulf Coast and other regions without a sustained cold winter dormancy period.

common_name: Mullica Queen Cranberry (Rutgers Late-Season High-Yield Processing Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring into strongly acidic, peaty, constantly moist bog soil topped with a sand layer, mimicking commercial cranberry bog conditions.

directions: Mullica Queen was released from the Rutgers P.E. Marucci Center cranberry breeding program in New Jersey's Pine Barrens and named for the Mullica River that runs through the region's historic bog country, joining Crimson Queen as one of the newer high-yield hybrids developed for the modern processing and juice trade. It ripens later in the season than most named cultivars, extending the harvest window for growers and giving berries additional time to build size and color, and it has shown good fruit-rot tolerance and vine vigor in New Jersey bog trials. Cultivation follows the same demanding requirements as all cranberries: acidic, peaty, constantly saturated soil (pH 4.0-5.0), a sand-topped bog bed, and full sun, with vines taking several years to establish before cropping heavily. As with other Rutgers 'Queen' series selections, it is grown almost exclusively in commercial New Jersey, Wisconsin, and Pacific Northwest bogs rather than home gardens, and is unsuited to warm-winter climates lacking sustained cold dormancy.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in acidic, peaty, moisture-retentive bog soil topped with sand; Franklin is an older Massachusetts hybrid grown mainly by heirloom and Cape Cod bog collections today.

directions: Franklin is a hybrid cranberry developed in the mid-twentieth century at the Massachusetts Agricultural Experiment Station's Cranberry Station in East Wareham, part of the same breeding effort on Cape Cod that produced Stevens and Pilgrim, at a time when growers needed hybrid vines with better vigor and disease tolerance than the old wild bog selections like Early Black and Howes. It bears small-to-medium, round, dark-red berries in modest but dependable yields, and while it was largely superseded commercially by the higher-yielding Stevens, it persists in heirloom bog collections and older Massachusetts marshes for its historical role in the state's cranberry breeding program. Grow it like any cranberry, in strongly acidic (pH 4.0-5.0), constantly moist, sandy-peat bog soil topped with a sand mulch layer to control weeds and encourage rooting along the runners. Vines need several years to establish a full crop but then persist and produce for decades with minimal care beyond steady moisture and acidic fertility. It is a cold-climate plant through and through, requiring a genuine winter dormancy and unsuited to Gulf Coast or other mild-winter regions.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in acidic, peaty, moisture-retentive bog soil topped with sand; Bergman is an older Wisconsin native-type selection grown mostly on legacy marshes rather than propagated as new commercial acreage today.

directions: Bergman is one of the 'native' Wisconsin cranberry selections, a naturally occurring bog vine identified and propagated directly from wild stock rather than produced through deliberate hybridization, in the same category as Searles and McFarlin among the varieties that predate the mid-century breeding programs. It has long been grown on older Wisconsin marshes for its reliable production and adaptability to local bog conditions, though its berries run smaller and less uniform than those of modern hybrid cultivars like Stevens, and it has been progressively replaced by higher-yielding hybrids on newly planted acreage. Culture is identical to other cranberries: strongly acidic (pH 4.0-5.0), constantly saturated, sandy-peat bog soil in full sun, with a sand top-dressing every few years to suppress weeds and refresh rooting surface for the spreading vines. Because it is a genuine cold-bog native selection, it needs a sustained winter dormancy and is not a candidate for warm-winter or Gulf Coast plantings. It remains of interest mainly to heirloom growers and Wisconsin cranberry marsh operations maintaining legacy plantings.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in acidic, peaty, moisture-retentive bog soil topped with sand; Grygleski #1 is a Wisconsin grower-selected hybrid grown mainly on regional marshes rather than distributed nationally.

directions: Grygleski #1 is a numbered hybrid selection that arose and was propagated within Wisconsin's cranberry marsh country, named for the Grygleski family, longtime Wisconsin cranberry growers and vine suppliers who identified and increased it for regional planting. It is grown almost exclusively on Wisconsin marshes rather than distributed as a national commercial release, valued locally for its vigor and productivity under the state's marsh soil and flood-management practices. Like other cranberries it must have strongly acidic, sandy-peat bog soil (pH 4.0-5.0) that stays constantly moist, full sun, and a periodic sand top-dressing to keep weeds down and encourage new rooting along the spreading vines. Establishing plantings takes several years before a full crop develops, after which vines can produce for decades with steady moisture and acidic fertility as the main ongoing inputs. As with all cranberries, it requires a real winter chill period and will not perform in warm-winter or Gulf Coast conditions.
